abstract: CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR-Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex1,2. Understanding the detailed mechanisms of this elaborate process is paramount to engineering CAST systems into programmable genetic tools3-6. Type I-F Pseudoalteromonas CAST (PseCAST) shows the highest activity in mammalian cells so far7 and has been adapted extensively through directed evolution8. However, its continued rational engineering requires addressing critical gaps in our understanding of transpososome assembly and activation9. Here we perform structural analyses using cryogenic electron microscopy, validated by DNA transposition assays, to visualize the PseCAST system in a series of functional states that define the stepwise mechanism of RNA-guided DNA integration. The structures of the PseCAST targeting and transposase recruitment complexes revealed that conformational changes in the Cascade-TniQ module, induced by R-loop formation, are associated with target-DNA stabilization and TnsC heptamerization. This, in turn, results in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase by conserved interactions with the carboxy-terminal tail of TnsB. Finally, the structure of the 1.2 MDa PseCAST transpososome holocomplex revealed allosteric coupling of TnsC-TnsB and TnsB-target-DNA interactions to the conformational remodelling of the TnsB catalytic site, activating donor-DNA integration. Together, these findings establish a unified mechanistic blueprint for RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs and provide a structural framework to guide their engineering for genome-editing applications.
